statement: In sleep-laboratory studies of people stopping after regular cannabis use or after daily high doses of THC, stopping is associated with worse sleep in the first week: pooling three small studies (about 38 people, editors' sum; Velzeboer et al., 2025; AMSTAR 2 critically low), sleep was shorter (standardized difference -0.79, 95% CI -1.16 to -0.42), took longer to start (1.21, 0.76 to 1.67) and was less efficient (-0.92, -1.38 to -0.46; two studies), with more REM (dream) sleep (1.61, 0.74 to 2.48) that began sooner (-1.09, -1.53 to -0.66), compared with sleep while still using. These are large standardized changes, but two of the three studies come from one 1970s laboratory that stopped high daily oral THC doses given in the study, the third is an uncontrolled before-and-after study of 20 people who were using cannabis and knew they had stopped, and the pooled data came from the first three days after stopping in two studies and days four to six in the third, so the review cannot say how long the changes last. The authors cite a suggestion that the very high oral THC doses in these studies may have made the REM rebound larger. Of all seven withdrawal studies reviewed, five found longer time to fall asleep, three shorter sleep (four found no change), three more waking in the night and three more REM sleep. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: When people who use cannabis a lot stop, their sleep gets worse for at least the first few nights. In sleep labs they slept less, took longer to fall asleep and woke more, and had more dream sleep, compared with when they were still using. These studies were small and old, and two of the three stopped very large lab doses. They did not check how long the bad sleep lasts after the first week.
population: Adults actively using cannabis (real-world use, one study of 20 people) or men with a history of daily use given high daily oral THC doses in a laboratory (two studies of 7 and 11 people)
exposure: Stopping cannabis or THC (doses are study conditions in the study card)
comparator: The same people's sleep while still using, or on THC before placebo substitution
outcome: Polysomnographic sleep in the first week after stopping
magnitude: Pooled standardized mean differences (95% CI): total sleep time -0.79 (-1.16 to -0.42), I-squared 0%; sleep onset latency 1.21 (0.76 to 1.67), 6.4%; sleep efficiency -0.92 (-1.38 to -0.46), two studies; REM sleep 1.61 (0.74 to 2.48), 46.8%; REM latency -1.09 (-1.53 to -0.66), 0%. Individual total sleep time estimates -0.95, -0.89 and -0.70.

evidence.extracted: Withdrawal meta-analyses of three studies: total sleep time -0.794 (-1.163 to -0.424), I-squared 0%; sleep onset latency 1.213 (0.757 to 1.669), 6.43%; REM sleep 1.609 (0.737 to 2.479), 46.8%; REM latency -1.092 (-1.527 to -0.657), 0%; sleep efficiency, two studies, -0.922 (-1.379 to -0.464), 0%. Individual studies for total sleep time: Feinberg 1975 -0.95, Feinberg 1976 -0.89, Vandrey 2011 -0.70.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Cannabis/Velzeboer_2025_SleepArchitectureMA.pdf (published version; forest plots and minus signs checked on rendered pages)

evidence.locator: Results 3.1.5, last two paragraphs (p. 9, right column); 3.2.1 to 3.2.3 (p. 10); 3.2.8 (p. 11)
evidence.extracted: Across all seven withdrawal studies: total sleep time fell in three and did not change in four; time to fall asleep rose in five; waking after sleep onset rose in three; REM rose in three. For the three pooled withdrawal studies, the data used came from the first three days in two and from days four to six in one.

evidence.locator: Table 1, withdrawal rows (p. 4); Table 2 (p. 5); Results 3.1.2, last paragraph (p. 8); Discussion, paragraph on REM rebound (p. 12)
evidence.extracted: Pooled withdrawal studies: Feinberg et al. 1975 (n = 7) and 1976 (n = 11), placebo substituted for daily high oral THC doses in experienced men, rated high risk of bias; Vandrey et al. 2011 (n = 20), sleep before and during abstinence in people actively using cannabis, aware they had stopped, rated low. The authors cite a suggestion (Bolla et al. 2010) that the REM rebound in these studies may be accentuated by their very high oral THC doses.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Cannabis/Velzeboer_2025_SleepArchitectureMA.pdf (published version; Tables 1 and 2 read on rendered pages)

risk_of_bias.note: Non-randomized designs; two of three pooled studies rated high risk; the third an open before-and-after comparison.

inconsistency.note: Pooled studies agree in direction; heterogeneity low except REM (46.8%).

indirectness.note: Two of three studies stop experimental high-dose oral THC, not real-world use; only the first week.

imprecision.note: About 38 people, but intervals exclude no change; the claim gives no precise size.

large_effect.note: Large standardized differences in small selected samples do not qualify (METHODS 6.3).

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; risk of bias -1 and indirectness -1 give very low (the floor). Status replicated: two independent laboratories (the 1970s group, with two studies, and a modern group) found the same direction. The narrative review by Angarita et al. (2016) describes the same withdrawal pattern second-hand and cites overlapping studies, so it is not independent support.
